title: Transactions and exactly-once
goal: By the end you can explain why consume-transform-produce duplicates output after a crash, make the outputs and the offset commit one Kafka transaction, predict what `read_committed` and `read_uncommitted` readers see and why the last stable offset holds them back, and say what fencing stops and where exactly-once ends.

warmup.q: A transactional producer writes 14 ledger entries, then aborts the transaction. A downstream consumer of the ledger topic uses default settings. What does it see?
options: Nothing: aborted records are deleted from the log
All 14 entries: the default `isolation.level` is `read_uncommitted`
Nothing: transactional records only reach the log on commit
The 14 entries, but only after `transaction.timeout.ms`
warmup.why: Transactional records are written to the log at once, before the decision; an abort only adds a marker. Hiding aborted records is the reader's job, and only a `read_committed` consumer does it. The default is `read_uncommitted`, which returns everything. The first and third options are the common belief that an abort removes or never writes the records.

sections.h: A crash between two writes duplicates the output
sections.body:
Most services in a payments platform do the same thing: read a record, work something out, write a record. The ledger service reads `payments` and writes a debit entry to `ledger-entries` for each payment. This read-transform-write shape is called **consume-transform-produce**.

Count the writes per batch. The entries go to `ledger-entries`. The group's new offset goes to `__consumer_offsets`, from lesson 6 of this track. Those are separate writes to separate partitions, possibly on separate brokers, and nothing ties them together. If the service dies after writing some entries and before committing the offset, the next instance starts at the old offset and writes those entries again. The Try-it shows it: instance 1 writes four entries and dies, and `ledger-entries` ends with 10 entries for 6 payments.

The idempotent producer from lesson 5 doesn't prevent this. It drops a retry of the same batch from the same producer session, recognised by producer id and sequence number. Instance 2 is a new producer with a new producer id, and its entries are new records.

Lesson 6 solved this problem at the far end: the ledger checks an idempotency key in the same database transaction as the balance update. That still works, but here it would have to be repeated in every consumer of `ledger-entries`: the balance service, the statement service, the reconciliation job. Each would need its own dedupe table.

Since both sides are Kafka, there is a better option. If the entries and the offset commit were one write, all of it or none of it, a crash couldn't leave half a batch behind. A Kafka **transaction** is that one write. It covers records sent to any number of partitions, plus the consumer group's offset commit, and it commits or aborts all of them together.

try.title: Crash a ledger service between its writes
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`.

Run `LedgerDemo` (command below). It writes six payments to a new topic. Instance 1 reads them, writes ledger entries for pay-0 to pay-3 to a second topic with a plain producer, and dies before it commits. Instance 2, in the same group, takes over.
Predict how many entries the output topic ends with, and which payments have two.

code.title: LedgerDemo.java

alt.title: LedgerDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
instance 1: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-3, then crashed before committing
instance 2: starts at offset 0
instance 2: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-5, committed offset 6
read_uncommitted reader sees 10 entries: {pay-0=2, pay-1=2, pay-2=2, pay-3=2, pay-4=1, pay-5=1}
read_committed   reader sees 10 entries: {pay-0=2, pay-1=2, pay-2=2, pay-3=2, pay-4=1, pay-5=1}
```
Instance 1's four entries reached the log; its offset commit never happened. Instance 2 started at offset 0 and wrote all six again: 10 entries for 6 payments. The two readers agree, because no transaction was involved: there is nothing for `read_committed` to hide.

sections.h: A transaction makes the entries and the bookmark one write

try.title: Run the same crash inside a transaction
steps: Run `LedgerDemo` with `txn` (command below). Instance 1 now writes its four entries inside a transaction, and instance 2 uses the same `transactional.id` and commits its entries and its offsets in one transaction.
Predict both lines at the end: what does the `read_committed` reader see, and what does the `read_uncommitted` one see?
try.expect:
```text
instance 1: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-3 inside a transaction, then crashed before committing
instance 2: initTransactions() aborted instance 1's open transaction
instance 2: starts at offset 0
instance 2: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-5, committed offset 6
read_uncommitted reader sees 10 entries: {pay-0=2, pay-1=2, pay-2=2, pay-3=2, pay-4=1, pay-5=1}
read_committed   reader sees  6 entries: {pay-0=1, pay-1=1, pay-2=1, pay-3=1, pay-4=1, pay-5=1}
```
The log holds the same 10 entries as before: the aborted four were not removed. The `read_committed` reader sees each payment exactly once, because instance 1's transaction was aborted and instance 2's entries became visible together with its offset commit. The `read_uncommitted` reader, the default, sees the duplicates anyway. The demo's consumers use `read_committed` too, which only matters when the input topic is itself written by transactions.

sections.h: read_committed readers stop at the last stable offset
sections.body:
The TxnDemo Try-it writes to one partition with a transactional producer and a plain one, and prints what two readers see. After a transaction commits `a` and `b`, the partition holds `a` at offset 0, `b` at 1, and the COMMIT marker at 2. Markers take an offset like records but are never returned by `poll`, so a reader sees offsets 0, 1 and then a gap. Next a transaction writes `c` and aborts: the log now holds `c` at offset 3 and an ABORT marker at 4. Whether a reader gets `c` depends on one consumer setting.

`isolation.level` decides. The default, `read_uncommitted`, returns every record, including those of aborted and still-open transactions. `read_committed` returns only records of committed transactions, plus all non-transactional records. Every consumer downstream of a transactional producer must set `read_committed`, or the transaction protects nothing: the default reader saw `c`.

A `read_committed` reader has a second rule. It can't read past the **last stable offset** (LSO): the first offset of the oldest transaction that is still open. Everything below the LSO is decided; at the LSO the broker doesn't know yet. In step 4 of the demo, an open transaction writes `e` at offset 6, and a plain producer then writes `f` at offset 7. `f` is not in any transaction, yet the `read_committed` reader stops at 6 and doesn't see it. Kafka returns records in offset order, so it can't hand out `f` while `e` is undecided. For that reader, `endOffsets` returns the LSO, and lag is measured to the LSO.

This is the price of transactions. A transaction that stays open holds back every `read_committed` reader of every partition it has written to, for every record behind it. A producer that crashes mid-transaction holds them until the coordinator aborts it after `transaction.timeout.ms` (60 seconds by default), or until a new instance with the same id calls `initTransactions`. Bugs used to leave some transactions hanging for good, with the LSO stuck and compaction blocked; KIP-890, finished in Kafka 4.0, added broker-side checks against that.

The stepper replays the ledger example on both partitions: the crash, the abort, the commit, and the LSO moving through them.

The six entries and the bookmark become visible at the same moment. A `read_committed` reader sees each payment's entry exactly once; a `read_uncommitted` reader sees all ten. That is the LedgerDemo `txn` run, step by step.

try.title: Watch markers, gaps and the last stable offset
steps: Run `TxnDemo` (command below). It writes to a new one-partition topic in five steps, with a transactional producer and a plain one, and after each step prints what a `read_uncommitted` reader and a `read_committed` reader get, and where each one stops (`endOffsets`).
Before step 4's lines, predict: does the `read_committed` reader see `f`, which no transaction wrote?

code.title: TxnDemo.java

alt.title: TxnDemo.kt
alt.src:
package sfz.kafka.l09.demo

import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Writes to a new one-partition topic with a transactional producer and a plain one, and after each step prints the
 * partition as a read_uncommitted reader and a read_committed reader see it: offsets, values, and where each stops.
 */
fun main() {
    val tp = TopicPartition("txn-demo-${System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000}", 0)
    val bootstrap = "localhost:9092"
    Admin.create(mapOf<String, Any>("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap)).use { it.createTopics(listOf(NewTopic(tp.topic(), 1, 1.toShort()))).all().get() }
    val ser = mapOf("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap, "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java, "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java)
    val txn = KafkaProducer<String, String>(ser + ("transactional.id" to "txn-demo"))
    val plain = KafkaProducer<String, String>(ser)
    fun send(p: KafkaProducer<String, String>, v: String) = p.send(ProducerRecord(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-1", v)).get()

    fun show(step: String) {
        println(step)
        for (isolation in listOf("read_uncommitted", "read_committed")) {
            KafkaConsumer<String, String>(
                mapOf("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap, "isolation.level" to isolation,
                    "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java, "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java),
            ).use { c ->
                c.assign(listOf(tp))
                c.seekToBeginning(listOf(tp))
                val end = c.endOffsets(listOf(tp)).getValue(tp) // read_committed: the last stable offset
                val seen = mutableListOf<String>()
                while (c.position(tp) < end) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach { seen += "${it.offset()}=${it.value()}" }
                println("  %-16s stops at %2d, sees %s".format(isolation, end, seen))
            }
        }
    }

    txn.initTransactions()
    txn.beginTransaction(); send(txn, "a"); send(txn, "b"); txn.commitTransaction()
    Thread.sleep(200) // the coordinator writes the markers just after the commit returns
    show("1. transaction commits a, b")
    txn.beginTransaction(); send(txn, "c"); txn.abortTransaction()
    Thread.sleep(200)
    show("2. transaction writes c, then aborts")
    send(plain, "d")
    show("3. plain producer writes d")
    txn.beginTransaction(); send(txn, "e")
    send(plain, "f")
    show("4. transaction writes e and stays open; plain producer writes f")
    txn.commitTransaction()
    Thread.sleep(200)
    show("5. transaction commits e")
    txn.close(); plain.close()
}

try.expect:
```text
1. transaction commits a, b
  read_uncommitted stops at  3, sees [0=a, 1=b]
  read_committed   stops at  3, sees [0=a, 1=b]
2. transaction writes c, then aborts
  read_uncommitted stops at  5, sees [0=a, 1=b, 3=c]
  read_committed   stops at  5, sees [0=a, 1=b]
3. plain producer writes d
  read_uncommitted stops at  6, sees [0=a, 1=b, 3=c, 5=d]
  read_committed   stops at  6, sees [0=a, 1=b, 5=d]
4. transaction writes e and stays open; plain producer writes f
  read_uncommitted stops at  8, sees [0=a, 1=b, 3=c, 5=d, 6=e, 7=f]
  read_committed   stops at  6, sees [0=a, 1=b, 5=d]
5. transaction commits e
  read_uncommitted stops at  9, sees [0=a, 1=b, 3=c, 5=d, 6=e, 7=f]
  read_committed   stops at  9, sees [0=a, 1=b, 5=d, 6=e, 7=f]
```
Offsets 2, 4 and 8 never appear: they are the COMMIT, ABORT and COMMIT markers. `c` at offset 3 reaches only the `read_uncommitted` reader. In step 4 the `read_committed` reader stops at 6, the LSO, so it misses `f` although no transaction wrote `f`. One commit later both readers end at 9.

sections.h: Zombies are fenced, but exactly-once ends at Kafka's edge
sections.body:
Instance A of the ledger service stops for 40 seconds: a long garbage-collection pause, or a network partition. The group decides A is gone (lesson 7), and instance B starts with the same transactional id. Then A wakes up and carries on where it was, with a transaction full of entries B has already written. A process that has been replaced but doesn't know it yet is called a **zombie**.

Kafka stops zombies with the epoch from lesson 5. Each `initTransactions()` bumps the epoch for its transactional id. The coordinator and the partition leaders remember the newest epoch and refuse anything sent with an older one. That is **fencing**. In the Try-it, A's next send fails with `InvalidProducerEpochException`, its commit fails the same way, and its abort fails with `ProducerFencedException`. The only thing left for A is to close. A reader sees A's committed work and B's, and nothing from A after the fence.

There is a second fence on the consumer side. `sendOffsetsToTransaction` takes `consumer.groupMetadata()`, which carries the member's generation, a counter the group moves on at every rebalance (lesson 7). If A was thrown out of the group, its generation is old, and the coordinator refuses its offsets even when the transactional ids differ (KIP-447). That is why one producer per instance is enough, instead of one per input partition. Since Kafka 4.0 (KIP-890), the producer also bumps its epoch at the end of every transaction, which closes gaps where a delayed message from an old transaction could land in a new one. That is why the epoch the Try-it prints jumps from 1 to 4 between A's commit and B's.

Now the boundary. A Kafka transaction covers records written to Kafka and offsets committed to Kafka, nothing else. Suppose the ledger service also calls the card issuer to capture a payment, or inserts a row into Oracle, inside the loop. On an abort-and-retry, the Kafka writes disappear from `read_committed` views, but the capture and the row don't. They run a second time on the retry. Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka. For a call or a database write inside the loop you still need lesson 6's tools: an idempotency key sent to the card issuer, or checked in the same database transaction as the effect.

Could Kafka take part in the database's transaction instead? KIP-939 proposes exactly that, two-phase commit with an external system, and it is accepted. It hasn't shipped: its client APIs were removed from the 4.1 and 4.2 release branches before release, and Kafka 4.4's `KafkaProducer` doesn't have them. Design as if it doesn't exist. Lesson 11 of this track shows the transactional outbox, the usual pattern for writing to a database and Kafka together.

try.title: Fence a zombie
steps: Run `ZombieDemo` (command below). Instance A commits one transaction, writes pay-2 in a second one and freezes. Instance B starts with the same `transactional.id` and redoes pay-2. Then A wakes up and tries to send, commit and abort.
Predict which of A's three calls fail, then run it.
Stop the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v`.

code.title: ZombieDemo.java

alt.title: ZombieDemo.kt
alt.src:
package sfz.kafka.l09.demo

import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Instance A of a ledger service has the transactional.id "ledger-0". It commits one transaction, opens another,
 * and then freezes, the way a long GC pause or a network partition freezes a process. Instance B starts with the
 * same transactional.id. Then A wakes up and carries on as if nothing happened.
 */
fun main() {
    val bootstrap = "localhost:9092"
    val tp = TopicPartition("zombie-demo-${System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000}", 0)
    val admin = Admin.create(mapOf<String, Any>("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap))
    admin.createTopics(listOf(NewTopic(tp.topic(), 1, 1.toShort()))).all().get()
    val config = mapOf<String, Any>("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap, "transactional.id" to "ledger-0",
        "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java, "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java)
    fun epoch() = admin.describeProducers(listOf(tp)).partitionResult(tp).get().activeProducers()
        .joinToString { "producer id ${it.producerId()} epoch ${it.producerEpoch()}" }

    val a = KafkaProducer<String, String>(config)
    a.initTransactions()
    a.beginTransaction(); a.send(ProducerRecord(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-1", "A: entry pay-1")); a.commitTransaction()
    println("A committed pay-1                              (partition 0 has seen ${epoch()})")
    a.beginTransaction(); a.send(ProducerRecord(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-2", "A: entry pay-2")).get()
    println("A wrote pay-2 in a new transaction, and freezes")

    val b = KafkaProducer<String, String>(config)
    b.initTransactions() // aborts A's open transaction and bumps the epoch: A is now a zombie
    b.beginTransaction(); b.send(ProducerRecord(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-2", "B: entry pay-2")); b.commitTransaction()
    println("B started with the same id, redid pay-2, committed (partition 0 has seen ${epoch()})")

    println("A wakes up:")
    try { a.send(ProducerRecord(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-3", "A: entry pay-3")).get() } catch (e: Exception) { println("  send:   ${e.cause?.javaClass?.simpleName}: ${e.cause?.message}") }
    try { a.commitTransaction() } catch (e: Exception) { println("  commit: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") }
    try { a.abortTransaction() } catch (e: Exception) { println("  abort:  ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") }
    a.close(Duration.ZERO) // fenced: the only thing left to do
    b.close()
    admin.close()

    KafkaConsumer<String, String>(
        mapOf("bootstrap.servers" to bootstrap, "isolation.level" to "read_committed",
            "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java, "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java),
    ).use { c ->
        c.assign(listOf(tp))
        c.seekToBeginning(listOf(tp))
        val seen = mutableListOf<String>()
        val deadline = System.nanoTime() + 5_000_000_000L
        while (seen.size < 2 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach { seen += it.value() }
        println("a read_committed reader sees: $seen")
    }
}

try.expect:
```text
A committed pay-1                              (partition 0 has seen producer id 7 epoch 1)
A wrote pay-2 in a new transaction, and freezes
B started with the same id, redid pay-2, committed (partition 0 has seen producer id 7 epoch 4)
A wakes up:
  send:   InvalidProducerEpochException: Producer attempted to produce with an old epoch.
  commit: InvalidProducerEpochException: Producer with transactionalId 'ledger-0' and (producerId=7, epoch=1) attempted to produce with an old epoch
  abort:  ProducerFencedException: There is a newer producer with the same transactionalId which fences the current one.
a read_committed reader sees: [A: entry pay-1, B: entry pay-2]
```
B kept A's producer id (it belongs to the transactional id) and moved the epoch on, so every call A made with its old epoch was refused. A's pay-2 entry was aborted when B started, and B's copy is the only one a `read_committed` reader sees. The producer id and epochs differ on your broker; a second run continues from the last epoch (6 and 9 on ours), because the transactional id `ledger-0` is the same.

refs.title: Commit removing the KIP-939 two-phase-commit APIs from the 4.2 branch

analogy: A transaction is like a bank teller's batch of slips for one customer: a withdrawal from one account, a deposit to another, and a note in the day book saying which request was handled. The teller writes all of them in pencil as she goes, and only at the end stamps the batch "approved" or "void". Auditors who read only stamped slips (`read_committed`) see the whole batch or nothing; a clerk who reads pencil too (`read_uncommitted`) sees voided slips. And while a batch is still in pencil, the careful auditors stop reading at its first slip, even past slips that are already in ink, because they read the book strictly in order. The analogy breaks at the bank's other systems: the stamp covers only slips in this book. If the teller also phoned another bank during the batch, voiding the slips doesn't undo the phone call.
in_your_world: Kafka transactions fit the Kafka-to-Kafka services in your platform: a fee calculator reading `payments` and writing `fees`, an enrichment step, a router that splits payments by currency. In Quarkus, the SmallRye connector does this with a `KafkaTransactions` emitter: `withTransactionAndAck` sends the outputs and the incoming message's offsets in one transaction, and the incoming channel needs `commit-strategy=ignore` so nothing else commits. Downstream channels set `isolation.level=read_committed`. Kafka Streams with `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` uses the same mechanism (lesson 10 of this track). The services that write to Oracle or call the card issuer are different: there the transaction covers only the Kafka side, so the idempotency key in Oracle from lesson 6 stays, and the issuer call must carry an idempotency key the issuer honours. If a Temporal workflow does the side effects, its activity retries need the same keys.
mistake: Turning on transactions in the producer and forgetting the readers. `isolation.level` defaults to `read_uncommitted`, so every downstream consumer that wasn't changed still sees aborted entries and the duplicates the transaction was meant to remove. Close behind: catching the failure, calling `abortTransaction()` and carrying on without rewinding the consumer, which silently skips the aborted batch; and calling a card issuer or writing to a database inside the transaction and assuming the abort undoes it. The fixes: `read_committed` on every consumer of a transactional topic, `seek` back to the batch's first offsets after every abort, and idempotency keys for every effect outside Kafka.

compare.note: The same calls in the same order. The catch order matters in both languages: `ProducerFencedException` is a `KafkaException`, so it must be caught first, or the code would try to abort with a fenced producer. Kotlin builds the offsets map with `associateWith` where Java fills a `HashMap`. Neither commits through the consumer: the offsets travel inside the transaction, which is why the consumer has `enable.auto.commit=false` and never calls `commitSync`.

steps.say: At start-up, call `initTransactions()` once. It aborts anything the previous pod with this id left open, so `read_committed` readers of `fees` aren't held at the LSO for the full 60-second timeout. Then run the batch loop from the compare block: one transaction per poll.

Sort the errors as the `KafkaProducer` javadoc does. `ProducerFencedException`, `OutOfOrderSequenceException`, `UnsupportedVersionException` and `AuthorizationException` are fatal: close the producer and let the pod restart. Any other `KafkaException`, including a `TimeoutException`, is abortable: abort, rewind, try the batch again. In the lab, `LedgerTransformer.processOnce` implements this and the broker test checks the fenced path.

Now the edge. If the fee service also posts the fee to an external billing API, that call isn't in the transaction: an abort and retry posts it twice. Send the payment's idempotency key with the call, so the billing API recognises the repeat, and keep the call idempotent on your side too. The Kafka transaction guarantees the `fees` topic and the offsets; the key covers the rest.
steps.code: billing.postFee(new FeeRequest(payment.idempotencyKey(), payment.account(), fee));   // same key on every retry

lab.title: Model the last stable offset, then build a transactional transformer
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 16 fail. `TxnPartitionTest` needs no broker; `LedgerTransformerTest` uses `MockConsumer` and `MockProducer`, which supports transactions; `TransactionsOnBrokerTest` runs against a Kafka 4.4 broker.

In `TxnPartition.kt`, write the model: `append` (a transactional record opens its producer's transaction if none is open), the private `end` behind `commit` and `abort` (a marker takes the next offset; remember the offset range of an aborted transaction), `lastStableOffset`, and `read` for both isolation levels. Several tests replay the TxnDemo run offset for offset.

In `LedgerTransformer.java`, write `init` and `processOnce`: begin, send the entries, `sendOffsetsToTransaction` with `consumer.groupMetadata()`, commit. On a `ProducerFencedException` rethrow it untouched; on anything else abort, seek every partition of the batch back to its first record, and rethrow.

Run everything until all 16 pass. The broker tests check that an aborted batch is invisible to `read_committed` and visible to `read_uncommitted`, that the retried batch appears exactly once, and that a second instance with the same transactional id fences the first.
hints: In the model, keep a map from producer id to the first offset of its open transaction. The LSO is the smallest value in it, or the log end when it is empty.
A record is hidden from `read_committed` if its producer's aborted range contains its offset; a marker is never returned to either reader.
Catch `ProducerFencedException` before `RuntimeException`: it extends `KafkaException`, which is a `RuntimeException`.

drill.title: The transactional batch from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, one consume-transform-produce batch in a transaction: begin, send one entry per record, add the offsets with the consumer's group metadata, commit; on a fenced producer rethrow; on any other `KafkaException` abort and rewind. Then answer: an open transaction's first record is at offset 120 of a partition whose log end is 180. Where does a `read_committed` reader stop, and what does `endOffsets` return for it?

recap: Consume-transform-produce makes separate writes (outputs, then offsets), so a crash between them duplicates output; the idempotent producer can't help across instances.
A transaction (`transactional.id`, begin, send, `sendOffsetsToTransaction`, commit) makes the outputs and the offset commit visible together, or not at all.
Records are in the log before the decision; COMMIT and ABORT markers decide, take an offset each, and leave gaps. Nothing is deleted on abort.
Only `read_committed` readers hide aborted records, and they stop at the last stable offset, the first offset of the oldest open transaction. The default is `read_uncommitted`.
`initTransactions` bumps the epoch and fences zombies; after an abort, rewind the consumer to the batch's start.
Exactly-once covers Kafka topics and offsets only. Calls and database writes inside the loop still need idempotency keys; KIP-939 two-phase commit has not shipped.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: the ledger's producer has idempotence on (the default) but no transactions. Instance 1 writes entries for pay-0 to pay-3 and crashes before committing offsets; instance 2 writes them again. Why does the broker accept the second copies?
options: Idempotence only dedupes within one batch
The broker only checks sequence numbers for `acks=1`
Instance 2 is a new producer session with a new producer id, so its records are new records
The broker does reject them; the duplicates come from the consumer
quiz.why: The idempotent producer drops a retry from the same producer id and sequence number. A restarted instance gets a new producer id, and its sends are not retries. A transactional id is what links instances across restarts: the new instance's `initTransactions` aborts the old one's open transaction instead of letting it stand.

quiz.q: A partition's log end is 151. A transaction that started at offset 100 is still open, and offsets 101 to 150 hold non-transactional records. What does a `read_committed` consumer get, and what is its end offset?
options: Offsets 101 to 150, end offset 151
Everything below 100, end offset 100: it waits for the transaction even for the plain records
Everything except offset 100, end offset 151
Nothing until the transaction commits
quiz.why: The last stable offset is the first offset of the oldest open transaction, 100. A `read_committed` reader never reads at or past it, because records are returned in offset order. `endOffsets` returns the LSO for such a reader. The plain records become visible once the transaction ends.

quiz.q: A transformer catches a `KafkaException` during a batch, calls `abortTransaction()`, and goes straight back to `poll`. What happens to that batch?
options: It is processed again in the next transaction
The broker replays it after the abort
Its entries are deleted from the output topic
It is skipped: the consumer's position is already past it, and only a restart would read it again from the committed offset
quiz.why: `poll` moved the position when it returned the batch (lesson 6). The abort hides the entries from `read_committed` readers and leaves the committed offset where it was, but the running consumer keeps reading from its position. Seek every partition back to the batch's first offset after an abort.

quiz.q: Instance A pauses for 40 seconds, the group moves on, and instance B starts with the same `transactional.id`. A wakes and calls `commitTransaction()`. What stops A's entries from becoming visible?
options: B's `initTransactions()` bumped the epoch; the broker refuses A's older epoch, so A's transaction can't commit
Nothing: A's commit succeeds and readers see duplicates
A's session timeout deletes its records
The consumer group rejects A's records
quiz.why: Fencing: each `initTransactions` gets a higher epoch for the id, and the coordinator and partition leaders refuse the older one. In Kafka 4.4 A's send and commit fail with `InvalidProducerEpochException` and its abort with `ProducerFencedException`; A must close. B's `initTransactions` also aborted whatever A had left open.

quiz.q: Inside a transactional batch, the fee service calls the billing API for each payment, then the batch's commit times out and the service aborts and retries the batch. What happens at the billing API?
options: Nothing: the abort rolls the calls back
The calls are made again for the retried batch, so fees are posted twice unless the API deduplicates by an idempotency key
Kafka holds the calls until the transaction commits
Kafka 4.4's two-phase commit makes the API part of the transaction
quiz.why: A Kafka transaction covers only Kafka writes and offsets. The HTTP calls already happened and happen again on the retry. Send the payment's idempotency key so the API recognises repeats. KIP-939's two-phase commit isn't in Kafka 4.4, and it would cover a database, not an HTTP API.

flashcards.front: What does a Kafka transaction make atomic in consume-transform-produce?
flashcards.back: The output records in any number of partitions plus the consumer group's offset commit (`sendOffsetsToTransaction`).

flashcards.front: When are a transaction's records written to the log?
flashcards.back: At once, when sent. Commit or abort only adds a marker; nothing is removed.

flashcards.front: What is the last stable offset (LSO)?
flashcards.back: The first offset of the oldest open transaction in a partition. `read_committed` readers never read at or past it.

flashcards.front: What is the default `isolation.level`, and what does it show?
flashcards.back: `read_uncommitted`: every record, including aborted and still-open transactions.

flashcards.front: What fences a zombie transactional producer?
flashcards.back: A new `initTransactions()` with the same `transactional.id` bumps the epoch; the broker refuses the old epoch.

flashcards.front: What must the code do after `abortTransaction()`?
flashcards.back: Seek the consumer back to the first offset of the batch in every partition, so the batch is processed again.

flashcards.front: Does a Kafka transaction cover a database write or an API call in the loop?
flashcards.back: No. Only Kafka writes and offsets. Use an idempotency key for the rest; KIP-939 two-phase commit hasn't shipped.

terms.plain: Read records, compute something, write records to another topic, and commit the input offsets.
A stable name for one producer instance, used to find its transaction coordinator and to fence older instances.
The broker that tracks a transactional id's transactions in `__transaction_state` and writes the markers.
A control record (COMMIT or ABORT) written into each partition a transaction touched; it takes an offset.
Consumer setting: `read_uncommitted` (default) returns everything; `read_committed` hides aborted and open transactions.
The first offset of the oldest open transaction; `read_committed` readers stop there.
An old instance that has been replaced but keeps running, for example after a long pause.
Refusing writes from an older epoch of a transactional id, so a zombie can't commit.

explain_back.prompt: Someone proposes turning on Kafka transactions in the ledger service so that "every payment is posted exactly once". The service reads `payments`, writes `ledger-entries`, and inserts a row into Oracle for each payment. Explain what transactions would and wouldn't guarantee, and what else is needed.
explain_back.answer: Transactions would make the Kafka side atomic: the entries written to `ledger-entries` and the group's offset commit on `payments` would become visible together or not at all, so a crash in the middle of a batch wouldn't leave duplicate entries for readers that use `read_committed`. We'd need a stable `transactional.id` per instance, so a restarted instance fences its predecessor and aborts its open transaction, a rewind after every abort, and `read_committed` on every consumer of `ledger-entries`, or they'd still see aborted entries. Transactions wouldn't cover the Oracle insert. If a batch is aborted and retried, the inserts from the first attempt are already committed in Oracle and would run again. So the Oracle side still needs lesson 6's idempotency key, checked by a unique constraint in the same database transaction as the insert. Kafka can't take part in Oracle's transaction: the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, hasn't shipped. And open transactions hold back `read_committed` readers at the last stable offset, so batches must stay short.

deeper.body:
**Why the epoch now moves on every commit.** Before Kafka 4.0, a transactional producer kept one epoch for its whole life. The EndTxn request that commits or aborts carried no sequence number, so a delayed commit or abort could arrive after the producer had already started its next transaction and be applied to the wrong one. Jepsen's 2024 analysis of Bufstream found this in Kafka's own protocol as aborted reads and lost writes (KAFKA-17754). KIP-890's second phase, finished in 4.0 and gated by the `transaction.version` feature, bumps the epoch at the end of every transaction and lets the broker add partitions to a transaction by itself, which closes that gap. The 4.0 upgrade notes also ask applications to abort on `TimeoutException` and `TransactionAbortableException`.

**How readers skip aborted records cheaply.** A `read_committed` fetch response carries a list of aborted transactions for the fetched range: producer id and first offset. The consumer drops records from those producers between that first offset and the matching ABORT marker. Brokers keep an index of aborted transactions next to each segment (the `.txnindex` file) so they can answer without scanning.

**Kafka Streams.** With `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`, Kafka Streams runs this lesson's loop for you: one transactional producer per stream thread, offsets and state-store changelog writes in the same transaction. The same edge applies: a Streams application that calls an external API inside a processor gets no exactly-once for that call.
